t: Fire programme: retention ₹20 lakh; 1st surplus 12 lines; 2nd surplus 8 lines; balance facultative. A risk of sum insured ₹5 crore suffers a loss of ₹75 lakh. The amount of the loss borne by the ceding insurer on its own account is
e: Retention ₹20 lakh is 20/500 of the risk. Cedant's share = 20/500 × ₹75 lakh = ₹3 lakh (1st surplus 36, 2nd surplus 24, facultative 12 lakh).

t: In the same programme (SI ₹5 crore; retention ₹20 lakh; 1st surplus 12 lines; 2nd surplus 8 lines), the 2nd surplus reinsurers' share of the ₹75 lakh loss is
e: 2nd surplus capacity = 8 × ₹20 lakh = ₹1.6 crore = 1.6/5 of the risk; share of loss = 1.6/5 × 75 = ₹24 lakh.

t: Retention on a risk is ₹10 lakh and the sum insured is ₹65 lakh. The cession to the surplus treaty amounts to
e: Surplus = ₹65 − ₹10 = ₹55 lakh; expressed in lines of ₹10 lakh this is 5.5 lines. Lines need not be whole numbers.

t: An insurer's maximum fire retention is ₹40 lakh but its retention schedule prescribes 50% of the maximum for inferior-class risks. Its surplus treaty is of 10 lines. For an inferior-class risk of sum insured ₹2.5 crore the facultative placement required is
e: Retention on this risk = ₹20 lakh; surplus capacity = 10 × ₹20 lakh = ₹2 crore; total automatic capacity ₹2.2 crore. Balance ₹30 lakh goes facultative — a lower retention also shrinks the treaty capacity because lines are multiples of the retention.

topic: Quota share with excess of loss
t: A 40% quota share treaty applies to the fire account and the insurer's net retained account is further protected by an XL cover of ₹30 lakh xs ₹10 lakh. A fire loss of ₹1 crore occurs. The insurer's final net loss is
e: Quota share reinsurer pays ₹40 lakh; net retained loss ₹60 lakh. XL pays the excess over ₹10 lakh up to ₹30 lakh. Cedant bears 10 + (60 − 40) = ₹30 lakh.

t: A stop loss cover pays 90% of losses in excess of a 75% loss ratio. Premium income is ₹80 crore and losses ₹70 crore. The recovery from reinsurers is
e: 75% of ₹80 crore = ₹60 crore; losses exceed this by ₹10 crore; reinsurers pay 90% of ₹10 crore = ₹9 crore.

t: Facilities (PML basis): obligatory cession 4%; net retention ₹3 crore; pool cession 25% max ₹10 crore; 1st surplus 8 lines max ₹24 crore; 2nd surplus 5 lines max ₹15 crore. A policy of sum insured ₹120 crore is underwritten at 50% PML. The facultative placement required is
e: PML amount = ₹60 crore. Obligatory 4% = 2.4; retention 3; pool 25% of 60 = 15 but max 10; 1st surplus 8 × 3 = 24; 2nd surplus 5 × 3 = 15. Total 54.4; facultative ₹5.6 crore.

t: GNPI for three years totalled ₹30 crore and losses to the XL cover ₹1.35 crore. Rate is burning cost loaded at 100/75, minimum 5%, maximum 7%. Current GNPI is ₹12 crore. The XL premium is
e: Burning cost = 1.35/30 = 4.5%; loaded = 4.5 × 100/75 = 6%, within the 5%–7% band. Premium = 6% of ₹12 crore = ₹72 lakh.

t: In the cover above (final premium ₹72 lakh) a deposit premium of ₹40 lakh was paid during the year. At adjustment the cedant
e: Adjusted premium ₹72 lakh less deposit ₹40 lakh = ₹32 lakh payable to reinsurers.

t: A policy for annual premium ₹12,000 is issued on 1 January. On 31 March the amounts of earned and unearned premium are respectively
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Written premium ₹12,000 is booked at issue; three of twelve months have expired, so earned premium is ₹3,000 and unearned premium (reserve for unexpired risk) is ₹9,000.

t: An XL cover of ₹80 lakh xs ₹20 lakh carries an annual premium of ₹4 lakh and one reinstatement at 50% additional premium, pro rata to amount only. A loss of ₹50 lakh ground-up occurs. The reinstatement premium is
e: Recovery = ₹30 lakh. RP = 30/80 × ₹4 lakh × 50% = ₹75,000.

topic: Reinstatement premium - pro rata to time
t: Treaty 1.4.2025 to 31.3.2026; cover ₹25 lakh xs ₹5 lakh; final XL premium ₹1,46,000; a ground-up loss of ₹40 lakh occurs on 1.2.2026; one reinstatement at 100% pro rata to amount and time. The reinstatement premium is
e: The recovery (₹25 lakh) exhausts the full limit, so the amount factor is 1. Unexpired days 1.2.2026 to 31.3.2026 = 28 + 31 = 59. RP = 1,46,000 × 59/365 = ₹23,600.

t: An XL layer of ₹2.5 crore xs ₹50 lakh is rated at 3% of GNPI ₹15 crore with one reinstatement at 100% (pro rata to amount). The year's only recovery was ₹50 lakh. A reinsurer with a 10% share has a
e: XL premium ₹45 lakh; reinstatement premium = 50/250 × 45 = ₹9 lakh. 10% share: 4.5 + 0.9 − 5 = profit ₹0.4 lakh = ₹40,000.

t: A buffer XL of ₹70 lakh xs ₹30 lakh has an aggregate deductible of 1.5% of GNPI; GNPI is ₹20 crore. Ground-up losses: ₹45 lakh, ₹50 lakh, ₹40 lakh and ₹1 crore. Total recovery is
e: Aggregate deductible ₹30 lakh. Excess over ₹30 lakh: 15, 20, 10 and 70 (limited to 70). Deductible absorbs 15 + 15; reinsurers pay 5 + 10 + 70 = ₹85 lakh.

topic: Catastrophe excess of loss - hours clause
t: A cat XL of ₹60 lakh xs ₹15 lakh per occurrence applies a 72-hours clause to riot within the limits of one city. Rioting in one city continues for five days: losses in the first 72 hours ₹55 lakh and in the remaining 48 hours ₹20 lakh. Recovery is
e: Two occurrences: 55 − 15 = ₹40 lakh and 20 − 15 = ₹5 lakh; total ₹45 lakh, each within the limit.

t: Treaty account (100%): premium ₹6,00,000; portfolio premium entry ₹2,40,000; portfolio loss entry ₹60,000; commission 42.5%; taxes ₹9,000; claims paid ₹2,10,000; premium reserve retained 40%; loss reserve retained 100% of outstanding losses ₹80,000. The balance due to a reinsurer with a 20% share is

First surplus fire treaty: premium ₹92 lakh; commission 45%; claims paid ₹24 lakh; taxes ₹30,000; management expenses 2.5%; portfolio entry premium 35% of previous premium ₹80 lakh and losses 100% of previous outstanding ₹20 lakh; portfolio withdrawal premium 35% of current premium and losses 100% of current outstanding ₹26 lakh. Profit commission at 20% is
A treaty pays 20% profit commission on profit up to 10% of ceded premium and 75% on the balance. Premium ceded ₹50 lakh; net profit ₹4 lakh. Profit commission is
e: 10% of premium = ₹5 lakh; the whole profit of ₹4 lakh falls within the first band, so commission = 20% of ₹4 lakh = ₹80,000; the 75% rate is not reached.

topic: Catastrophe XL - rate on line and payback
t: A cat XL layer of ₹80 crore is bought for a premium of ₹4 crore. The payback period implied by this pricing is
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Rate on line = 4/80 = 5%; payback period = 1 ÷ rate on line = 20 years, i.e. one full-limit loss is expected to be recouped over 20 years of premium.

t: Profit commission is 20% with deficits carried forward until extinguished. Year 1 loss ₹8 lakh; year 2 profit ₹5 lakh; year 3 profit ₹9 lakh. Profit commission payable in year 3 is
e: Year 2: 5 − 8 = −3, no commission, deficit ₹3 lakh carried forward. Year 3: 9 − 3 = ₹6 lakh × 20% = ₹1.2 lakh.

t: Earned premium ₹2,00,000; losses paid ₹1,10,000; outstanding losses carried forward ₹50,000; outstanding losses brought forward ₹30,000. The incurred loss ratio is
The obligatory cession to the Indian reinsurer was reduced from 20% to 15% in
e: Statutory cession: 20% until 2006-07, 15% in 2007-08, 10% from 2008-09, 5% from 2013-14 and 4% from 2022-23.

t: Reinsurance helps an insurer absorb new risk exposures arising from all of the following EXCEPT
e: Reinsurance absorbs underwriting exposures (new technology, new covers, new classes); currency fluctuation is a financial risk outside the reinsurance function.

t: Companies to which a licence is sold by reinsurance companies to participate in their business are called
e: Fronting companies lend their licence/paper to write business which is then largely reinsured to the party that actually bears the risk.

t: Insurance companies formed by large industrial or commercial groups to meet the insurance needs of their parent are called
e: A captive is owned by its insureds (the parent group); it typically buys reinsurance to protect its own retention.

t: Premiums ceded ₹5,00,000; premium reserve brought forward ₹1,80,000; premium reserve carried forward ₹2,10,000. Earned premium is
e: ★ Key fact (repeated across the mocks of this paper). Earned premium = 5,00,000 + 1,80,000 − 2,10,000 = ₹4,70,000.

t: Regional reinsurance companies can retrocede their business by means of
e: Retrocession uses the same techniques as reinsurance: quota share/surplus retrocession treaties as well as XL protections.

t: Under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, an inward treaty agreement received from a foreign ceding company
o: is exempt from Indian stamp duty
is stamped by the foreign cedant
is stamped only if the premium exceeds ₹1 crore
requires to be stamped in India
e: Inward treaties from foreign cedants must be stamped in India; for outward treaties the copy retained in India is stamped.

t: In marine hull reinsurance the treaty form more commonly used is
e: Hull values vary widely per vessel, so surplus treaties (often combined with XL) are common; cargo more often uses quota share with surplus.

t: Which of the following is correct about accounting by insurers and reinsurers?
o: statutory accounting is the only system they are subject to
GAAP accounting is prohibited for reinsurers
statutory accounting is not the only system; publicly traded companies also report under GAAP
reinsurers need not prepare statutory accounts
e: Besides statutory accounting required by regulators, insurers and reinsurers also report under GAAP or IFRS where their capital is publicly traded.

t: A 'risk profile' supplied to reinsurers is
o: a list of claims above the priority
statistics of numbers of risks and/or premium split into bands of sums insured
e: The risk profile shows the distribution of the portfolio by sum insured band and is used by XL underwriters for exposure rating.

t: Loss adjustment expenses that can be identified with a specific claim file (such as attorney's fees) are called
e: ALAE are claim-specific expenses; ULAE are general claims department costs such as salaries, which are not charged to individual files.

t: The subject premium to which an XL rate is applied is described as 'gross/net' because it is
o: gross of commission and net of taxes
net of commission and gross of claims
gross of all reinsurance and net of claims
gross before deducting the XL premium itself but net of other reinsurances, cancellations and refunds
e: GNWPI/GNEPI is gross of the reinsurance under consideration but net of other adjustments such as returns, cancellations and other reinsurance premiums.

t: A fire portfolio has no proportional treaty. To limit its commitment on any single risk the insurer may use a facultative excess of loss cover, and as an alternative to a proportional treaty it may use
o: a working (risk) excess of loss treaty
e: Working risk XL protects the net retention against large individual losses and can replace a surplus treaty where the cedant wishes to keep more premium.

t: An insurer's crop account suffers an unusually high frequency of small claims in a year, none exceeding its per-risk retention. The cover that protects its annual result in this situation is
e: Per-risk XL does not respond to many small losses below the priority; stop loss protects the loss ratio of the whole class for the year.

t: Which of the following does NOT influence an insurer's retention limit?
o: the number of employees in the claims department
the company's capital and net worth
e: Retention depends on financial strength (assets, capital, free reserves), portfolio size and spread, and management attitude; staffing has no bearing.

t: Section 41 of the Insurance Act 1938 prohibits:
o: Payment of any rebate of premium or commission as an inducement to buy insurance
Issue of a policy without a medical examination
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). Section 41 bars rebating; contravention attracts a penalty of up to ₹10 lakh.

t: A fire retention schedule normally grades risks by
o: location/separation, class of construction and fire protection, and process carried on
e: Property retention schedules reflect physical hazard: construction, protection, separation and occupancy/process determine how much the insurer keeps.

t: Profit commission under a surplus treaty is allowed by the reinsurer when
o: the cedant's company as a whole makes a profit
the treaty itself results in a profit for the reinsurer
e: Profit commission is a share of the reinsurer's profit on that treaty, computed through a profit commission statement; the cedant's overall results are irrelevant.

t: Where quota share and surplus treaties are combined to protect a class, the order of cession is
o: quota share first, then surplus on the balance
at the cedant's choice on each risk
e: The quota share applies to the gross acceptance first; the retained portion after quota share is then protected by the surplus treaty.

t: For marine and aviation treaties the reinsurer's emphasis in acceptance is mainly on
o: the construction of each vessel or aircraft
the reputation of the cedant and its previous results
e: Marine and aviation treaties are judged on the cedant's underwriting reputation and track record rather than on individual risk details.

t: Under a proportional treaty the renewal of cessions on expiring policies is
o: subject to the reinsurer's discretion each year
e: Treaty reinsurance is obligatory and continuous; cessions renew automatically with the original policies as long as the treaty is in force.

t: Section 64VB of the Insurance Act 1938 requires that:
o: Premium is received in advance before the risk is assumed
Every policy carries a free-look clause
e: ★ Core fact (asked across III papers). No risk may be assumed unless the premium has been received in advance or is guaranteed in the manner prescribed.

t: A reinsurer's reputation in the market is built on
o: the number of its branch offices
the size of its brokerage payments
its ability to influence rates, terms and conditions, its underwriting capacity and its expertise
its willingness to accept all risks offered
e: Lead reinsurers earn their standing through capacity, expertise and the ability to set market terms.

t: The period during which treaty terms are settled and the reinsurers' percentage participations are determined is called the
e: During the negotiation (renewal) period the slip is finalised and lines are written; the reinsurance period is the contract term that follows.

t: The benefit-to-cost ratio of a reinsurance programme is calculated as
o: total loss recovered divided by net cost of reinsurance
ceded premium divided by paid losses
paid losses divided by ceded premium
net retention divided by ceded premium
e: Benefit-to-cost ratio = total recoveries ÷ net cost of reinsurance (ceded premium less commissions and recoveries) and measures the value obtained from the programme.

t: Under a liability XL treaty all claims arising from the manufacture or distribution of one faulty batch of a product are
o: treated as separate losses, each subject to the priority
treated as one loss only if reported within 72 hours
aggregated and treated as one loss occurrence
e: Liability treaties define one occurrence to include all claims from one faulty batch or lot, just as occupational disease claims in one policy period are aggregated.

t: Accounts under a proportional fire treaty are normally rendered
e: Treaty accounts are rendered periodically (usually quarterly, sometimes monthly or half-yearly) within the time frame set by the accounting clause.

t: Accumulation of risk across different branches of an insurer is most likely in
e: PA, liability and aviation exposures from different branches can be hit by one event (e.g. an air crash), so per-event retention must be controlled centrally.

t: Under an XL treaty covering fidelity guarantee on a losses-discovered basis, 'one loss' is usually limited to
o: losses discovered in one calendar month
the acts of one individual, or of more than one if acting in collusion
losses of one policyholder in one year
e: Fidelity losses are aggregated per dishonest employee (or per group acting in collusion), which defines the unit tested against the priority.
